title: What is the best tile side called, and how many tiles cover the floor?
description: The largest common factor of twelve and sixteen is given its name. Then the plan is divided into rows and columns of tiles, and the tiles along each wall are counted before they are multiplied. Keeko's doubt, adding the tiles along two walls, is tested on the plan.
teaching_notes: One idea: the largest common factor is the highest common factor, and the tiles on a floor are the tiles along one wall times the tiles along the other. Watch for students who add the two wall counts instead of multiplying them.

source: Name the largest common factor of 12 and 16, and find how ma
video_script.why: The child has the largest common factor of twelve and sixteen but not yet its name, or the count of tiles it gives.
video_script.substitution: Dividing each wall by the tile side gives the tiles in a row and in a column, and the floor holds that many rows of that many tiles.
video_script.anchor: The room of the book, twelve feet by sixteen feet, tiled with the largest square tile that fits.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the three tiles along one wall to the four along the other and says seven tiles. That counts only one edge of tiles along each wall, not the rows that fill the floor.

final_answer.spoken: the highest common factor is four and twelve tiles are needed

names.{{NAME_1}}: builds a new house and tiles the main room (12 ft by 16 ft)

maths_rules: Common factors of 12 and 16: 1, 2, 4. Largest is 4, so HCF(12, 16) = 4.
Tiles on the floor: 3 rows of 4 tiles, 3 x 4 = 12.
Slip: 3 + 4 = 7 counts only the tiles along two walls; the floor needs 3 x 4 = 12.
video_script.design: One idea: the HCF is the side of the largest tile, and the floor holds rows times tiles in a row. Assumes common factors of twelve and sixteen are known. Wrong idea: adding the two wall counts. The plan stays all video.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the room of {{NAME_1}}.
<bookmark mark='room'/>The room is twelve feet by sixteen feet, and the best square tile is laid on the floor.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the side of that tile called, and how many such tiles cover the floor?

beats.on_screen: the plan and the questions stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: tiles laid edge to edge along the short wall and the long wall of the plan; the rest of the floor fills with rows of tiles

marks.edge: Tiles are laid edge to edge along each wall
marks.rows: The floor fills with rows and columns of tiles

narration: <bookmark mark='edge'/>Square tiles are laid edge to edge along each wall of the room.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Across the floor they form rows and columns. The number of tiles is the tiles in a row times the number of rows.

beats.on_screen: Given: room 12 ft by 16 ft; square tiles that fit both walls exactly

marks.given: The two wall lengths are written under Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the room is twelve feet by sixteen feet, and the square tiles fit both walls exactly.

beats.on_screen: To find: the name of the largest common factor of 12 and 16; the number of tiles

marks.find: The words To find are written under Given

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to name the largest common factor of twelve and sixteen, and count the tiles.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: common factors of 12 and 16: 1, 2, 4; largest = 4; highest common factor (HCF) of 12 and 16 = 4

marks.common: The common factors one, two and four are written
marks.name: The largest is circled and the name highest common factor, HCF, is written beside it

beats.colours: the largest number in the highlight colour
narration: <bookmark mark='common'/>Step one, take the common factors of twelve and sixteen. They are one, two and four.
<bookmark mark='name'/>The largest common factor is called the highest common factor, or H C F. For twelve and sixteen it is four.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: tiles along the 12 ft wall = 12 / 4 = 3

marks.short: Three tiles are counted along the short wall

narration: <bookmark mark='short'/>Step two, divide the short wall by the tile side to count the tiles along it. Twelve divided by four gives three tiles.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: tiles along the 16 ft wall = 16 / 4 = 4

marks.long: Four tiles are counted along the long wall

narration: <bookmark mark='long'/>Step three, divide the long wall by the tile side in the same way. Sixteen divided by four gives four tiles.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 3 rows of 4 tiles; number of tiles = 3 x 4

marks.rows: The floor is shown as three rows of four tiles
marks.times: The product sign joins three and four

narration: <bookmark mark='rows'/>Step four, the floor is three rows of four tiles. <bookmark mark='times'/>Multiply three by four to count every tile on the floor.

marks.ans: The answer is boxed in the highlight colour

beats.colours: the answer in the highlight colour
narration: The highest common factor is four, and {{NAME_1}} needs twelve tiles of that size.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the plan
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 3 + 4 = 7 tiles; only the tiles along two walls are filled in and the middle of the floor stays bare; the bubble is struck through

beats.colours: the wrong idea in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks seven tiles are enough. Three tiles on one wall and four on the other make seven.
<bookmark mark='edge'/>That counts only the tiles along two walls.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The middle of the floor is still bare. The floor needs three full rows of four tiles.
